analysis.one_liner: Caps what Medicare seniors pay for prescription drugs at the government's lowest negotiated price.
analysis.headline: A bill promising to cut Medicare seniors' drug prices by more than 40 percent gathered 153 House cosponsors but never got a vote in any committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug companies that sell to the federal government to sell the same drugs to pharmacies, for Medicare patients, at the lowest price the government itself pays. Seniors buying their own prescriptions often pay far more than insurers or government programs pay for the very same drugs, so this would have cut their out-of-pocket costs sharply. The bill was referred to two House committees and died in subcommittee without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, most of whom had no prescription drug coverage in 1999 and paid cash at the pharmacy. The bill's findings say older Americans who buy their own drugs pay on average twice as much as the government's favored customers, sometimes over 15 times more, and that more than one in eight seniors have to choose between food and medicine. It also would have extended lower prices to seniors in hospice care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare paying cash for drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires participating drug manufacturers to sell covered outpatient drugs to pharmacies, in quantities matched to what the pharmacy sells to Medicare beneficiaries, at the lower of the lowest federal price or the manufacturer's best price, which the bill's findings estimate would cut seniors' drug prices by more than 40 percent.
Extends the same pricing to drugs furnished to Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare-certified hospice programs, covering terminally ill patients.
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to issue regulations, report to Congress within two years and annually on whether the law actually reduced prices, and recommend further changes.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose bill findings say the discriminatory pricing sustains about $20 billion a year in profits. Pharmacies would buy at lower wholesale prices and pass the savings to seniors. Any revenue loss to drug companies could in principle reduce funds available for research and development.

drawbacks.text: The bill works only on manufacturers that contract with the United States; a company could avoid the price mandate by exiting federal sales, so coverage would depend on firms staying in the market.

Price controls on brand-name drugs reduce manufacturer revenue; an honest supporter would acknowledge this could shrink funds for developing new medicines, though the bill's findings argue the gains to seniors' health and to taxpayers outweigh that.
It is a price mandate, not a Medicare drug benefit: seniors would still pay out of pocket for every prescription, just at a lower price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: tens of billions of dollars in savings for seniors who were paying retail prices with no coverage, on drugs the government already buys cheaply through Medicaid and the VA. The main cost falls on drug company profits, which the industry would argue threatens innovation, and the bill's mandatory-price structure was untested. On balance this was a straightforward transfer of pricing power from manufacturers to Medicare patients, but it never advanced far enough to be modified or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to their health subcommittees, and sat there for the rest of the Congress without a markup or floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 1999, and referred to the House Commerce Committee and, in addition, the Ways and Means Committee.
In late February and March 1999 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment and the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, where the action history ends.
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the bill repeatedly through 2000, including on May 19, 1999 and June 19, 2000, but no committee or floor vote is recorded.
The bill ended the 106th Congress without a vote; the bill's own findings projected it would cut Medicare beneficiaries' drug prices by more than 40 percent.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers kept full pricing freedom over Medicare patients, who continued paying retail drug prices with no federal drug benefit.

for.name: Rep. Tom Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and returned to the floor repeatedly through 2000 to make the case for it.

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only non-Democrat on the list.

against.name: Rep. Thomas J. Bliley Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup of the bill after its referral to the committee.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup after the bill was also referred to Ways and Means.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed government price mandates on drug prices and campaigned against Medicare price-control proposals in 1999-2000.

sides.party_line_note: All 153 cosponsors were House Democrats plus one Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican committee chairs never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill would have forced manufacturers that sell to the federal government to extend their lowest government price to pharmacies serving Medicare patients, cutting the roughly $20 billion in annual profits the bill says discriminatory pricing sustains. Drug companies' pricing power over seniors buying at retail was exactly what the bill targeted.

Pharmacies would have bought drugs at lower wholesale prices and been guaranteed supply equal to what Medicare patients buy, but the bill does not say how their margins would be preserved. In practice they would have passed most of the savings through to senior customers.

Hospice drug purchases for Medicare enrollees were counted in the pricing formula and the lower prices would have extended to terminally ill patients, lowering costs for hospice care programs and their patients.
